newsitem.title: USA: US Senate panel to weigh '95 litigation reform.
newsitem.headline: US Senate panel to weigh '95 litigation reform.

text.p: A Senate Banking panel next week will hear the concerns of technology companies and others who fear they are still exposed to meritless securities class action lawsuits, despite 1995 reforms by Congress.

The Senate Banking Committee's Securities Subcommittee, chaired by Texas Republican Phil Gramm, will hear the views of the Securities and Exchange Commission, state securities regulators, technology industry representatives and others on how Congress' 1995 federal securities litigation reforms have worked.
"The focus of the hearing will be to review how the 1995 Act has played out and to what extent it has solved the problems or achieved the goals set by Congress," a Senate aide said.

Some industry sources say the July 24 hearing will likely be a precursor to legislation to be introduced this fall by Gramm and Sen. Christopher Dodd, D-Conn., the ranking Democrat on the panel, that would make it even more difficult for securities class action suits to make their way into courts, including state courts.
Consumer advocates, state and local government representatives and others say Congress' 1995 reforms left investors with little protections and have warned against setting more curbs.

But the Uniform Standards Coalition, a nationwide organization of high-tech companies and venture capitalists, has been urging lawmakers for more reforms, claiming that litigators have been able to get around the 1995 reforms by moving securities class actions to state courts.
The group has lobbied Congress for protections against such suits when companies provide investors with forward-looking statements about a company's performance.

"If you have a handful of state cases it totally undercuts the safe harbor," said Mark Gitenstein, the coalition's executive director. "You only need really one case that you can sue a company for making a forward looking statement, which is at the heart of these technology and growth companies when they go into the capital markets."

Others invited to testify at the July 24 hearing include the Securities Industry Association, the National Association of Securities and Commercial Law Attorneys, former SEC Commissioner Joseph Grundfest, and California's state securities regulator.
Investor and consumer groups would be asked to testify in the Fall if legislation is introduced, the Senate aide said.
